title: A hundred years asleep
hookLine: a man passes a ruined town, dies a hundred years, and wakes to see his donkey raised (2:259)
carry: he can revive what is dead

lines: HOW COULD THIS EVER LIVE AGAIN?
cards: A traveler rides his donkey past a town that's been destroyed: roofs fallen in, walls collapsed onto themselves, nobody left. He's carrying some food and something to drink.

He stops, looks at the ruins, and says what anyone might say: how could God ever bring this back to life? The text doesn't say whether he asks it in wonder or in doubt. And then, the Qur'an says, he finds out.

teach.h: A DAY, OR PART OF A DAY
teach.b: Verse two hundred fifty-nine goes on: God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him, and asked: how long have you stayed? He answered: a day, or part of a day. That's how waking feels.

teach.h: THE FOOD UNSPOILED, THE DONKEY RAISED
teach.b: Look at your food and drink: they haven't spoiled. Look at your donkey. And look at the bones, how We set them together and clothe them with flesh.
When it became clear to him, he said: I know that God has power over all things.

The Qur'an doesn't name the man or the town. The commentators offer names: some say 'Uzayr, whom some identify with Ezra, and the town Jerusalem after its destruction; others name the prophet Jeremiah, or someone else.
The story works without a name. Look at the details it does give. The food is unchanged after a century.

The donkey, in one reading, has gone to bones and comes back; other commentators read the bones as the man's own. One thing time didn't touch, one thing it took completely, and in the story both are in God's hands.
And look where the story sits. Just before it, Ibrahim tells a king: my Lord gives life and causes death. Just after it, Ibrahim asks to see how the dead are raised, and is shown with four birds.
Three stories in a row about the same question. The man's question isn't scolded. It's answered with a demonstration he lives through.

how: Muslims read 2:258–260 together as three stories about God giving life to the dead, and often recall them when speaking of resurrection and of hope after loss.

games.q: you stand before a ruined town and ask: how could God ever bring this back to life? what happens to you in the story?
o: you're shown: made to die a century, then raised.
games.why: the question is answered, vividly: a hundred years, food unspoiled, a donkey raised from bones. he ends: I know God has power over all things.

practice: Bring to mind something old coming back to life, a tree leafing after winter, a friendship starting again, a skill returning to your hands, and look closely at what was dead and what's stirring now.
If you pray, hold it up with the man's last words: I know that God has power over all things.

wordCard.voice: 'Uzayr. The name some commentators give the man who doubted a ruined town could live, was made to die a century, and woke to see his donkey raised. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a hundred years, the span the man was made to die in 2:259.

carryVoice: Your line: he can revive what is dead. A ruin isn't the end of the story. See you tomorrow.
